title: The Extended and Embodied Mind
subtitle: Where does your mind stop and the rest of the world begin?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain the extended mind thesis, the parity principle and the case of Otto's notebook.
By the end you will be able to state the conditions Clark and Chalmers proposed for genuine extension and the objections of Adams and Aizawa and of Rupert.
By the end you will be able to describe embodied cognition and enactivism and how they challenge the computational picture of Lesson 1.
By the end you will be able to assess whether smartphones and AI assistants can be parts of our minds, and what follows if they are.
hook:
Try multiplying 347 by 28 in your head. Now try it with a pencil and paper. With the paper, you write down partial results, carry digits, line up columns. The paper is not just recording a calculation your brain has done; it is doing part of the work, holding what your working memory cannot. Is the paper, during those seconds, part of your thinking?

The computational picture of Lesson 1 placed the mind inside the head, as software running on the brain's hardware. Descartes (Day 44) went further, placing it outside the physical world altogether. In 1998 Andy Clark and David Chalmers published a short paper in the journal *Analysis* that asked a provocative question: "Where does the mind stop and the rest of the world begin?" Their answer, that the mind can literally extend into notebooks, tools and devices, launched one of the liveliest debates in philosophy of mind. And at a time when billions of people carry their memories, maps and calendars in their pockets, the question has never been more practical.

sections.heading: Otto's Notebook and the Parity Principle
sections.body:
Clark and Chalmers built their case around a thought experiment. **Inga** hears that there is an exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art. She thinks for a moment, recalls that the museum is on 53rd Street, and walks there. Everyone agrees that Inga believed, even before she recalled it, that the museum was on 53rd Street: the belief was stored in her memory, waiting to be accessed.

**Otto** has Alzheimer's disease. Like many people with memory impairments, he relies on a notebook that he carries everywhere, writing down new information and looking up old information. He hears about the exhibition, consults his notebook, which says the museum is on 53rd Street, and walks there.

Clark and Chalmers argued that Otto, too, believed the museum was on 53rd Street before he looked it up. The notebook plays the same role for Otto that biological memory plays for Inga. The information is reliably there, he trusts it, he consults it automatically, and it guides his actions in the same way. The only difference is that one store is inside the skull and the other is outside. Why should that make a difference?

The argument rests on what they called the **parity principle**:

> If, as we confront some task, a part of the world functions as a process which, were it done in the head, we would have no hesitation in recognizing as part of the cognitive process, then that part of the world is (so we claim) part of the cognitive process.

Notice how naturally this follows from functionalism (Lesson 1). If mental states are defined by their roles, not by what they are made of, then location should not matter either. If silicon can realize a belief, why not ink?

Clark and Chalmers called their view **active externalism**, to distinguish it from an older externalism associated with Hilary Putnam and Tyler Burge. Putnam's "Twin Earth" argument (1975) held that the *meaning* of our words depends partly on our environment ("meanings just ain't in the head"), but the environment in that case is distant and passive. In the extended mind, the external parts are active, doing causal work in the here and now, coupled to the brain in a loop.

sections.heading: Conditions for Extension, and the Critics
sections.body:
If every external resource counted as part of the mind, the view would quickly become absurd. Do you believe everything in the library? Everything on the internet? Clark and Chalmers proposed conditions that a resource must meet to count as part of a person's cognitive system, conditions that Otto's notebook satisfies:
1. It is **reliably available** and typically invoked.
2. Information retrieved from it is more or less **automatically endorsed**, not usually subjected to critical scrutiny.
3. It is **easily accessible** when required.
4. The information was **consciously endorsed** at some point in the past, and is there because of this endorsement. (They were less certain about this condition.)

A library book you have never read fails conditions 1, 2 and 4. A notebook you carry everywhere passes.

Critics raised three main objections.

**The coupling-constitution fallacy.** Fred Adams and Kenneth Aizawa (*The Bounds of Cognition*, 2008) argued that Clark and Chalmers confuse causal coupling with being a part. Just because a process is causally connected to cognition does not make it cognitive. An air conditioner is coupled to a room's temperature, but it is not part of the temperature. Adams and Aizawa argued that cognition requires a **mark of the cognitive**: in particular, states with **non-derived content**, meaning that is intrinsic rather than borrowed from an interpreter. The ink marks in Otto's notebook mean something only because Otto interprets them; the representations in Inga's brain do not depend on any interpreter.

**The embedded alternative.** Robert Rupert (2004) argued for the **embedded** mind: cognition depends heavily on the environment, but cognitive systems are still located in the organism. Otto uses an external tool, just as a person uses glasses; that makes the notebook important to his cognition, not part of it. Rupert argued that cognitive science gains nothing from the extension and loses the stable, persisting organism as its object of study.

**Cognitive bloat.** If Otto's notebook is part of his mind, what about his phone, his search engine, or his spouse who remembers things for him? Extension threatens to spread the mind everywhere. Clark and Chalmers bit the bullet in some cases: they suggested that in some close relationships, a partner might function as part of one's memory.

Defenders replied that Adams and Aizawa's mark of the cognitive is too strict: much of the brain's own processing, such as early visual processing, may lack anything like the right sort of content, yet no one denies it is cognitive. And Clark has argued that the real question is not where the boundary lies but how the brain integrates internal and external resources into a single problem-solving system. Clark and Chalmers also proposed a vivid empirical example: in experiments by David Kirsh and Paul Maglio, Tetris players physically rotated pieces on the screen to see whether they fit, because this was faster than rotating them mentally. The rotation on screen was part of the player's thinking, not just its output.

sections.heading: Embodied Cognition: Thinking with the Body
sections.body:
The extended mind thesis says cognition can spread outward into tools. A broader family of views, often grouped as **4E cognition** (embodied, embedded, enacted and extended), says that cognition is shaped, at a deep level, by the body and its interactions with the world.

**Embodied cognition** holds that the body is not just an input-output device for a central computer; the details of our bodies shape the concepts we have and the way we think. George Lakoff and Mark Johnson, in *Metaphors We Live By* (1980), argued that abstract thought is structured by bodily metaphors: we understand time as space ("looking forward to the weekend"), affection as warmth ("a cold reception"), understanding as grasping ("I see", "I get it").

This idea has roots in the **phenomenology** you met on Day 75. The French philosopher Maurice Merleau-Ponty, in *Phenomenology of Perception* (1945), argued against Descartes that the primary way we are in the world is not as a thinking thing but as a **lived body**, skilled and active. His example of a blind man's cane is a precursor of the extended mind: for a practiced user, the cane is no longer an object he perceives; he perceives *through* it, feeling the pavement at its tip. The cane has become part of his perceptual system. Similarly, an experienced driver feels the width of the car as if it were her own body.

**Enactivism**, launched by Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson and Eleanor Rosch in *The Embodied Mind* (1991), goes further. It holds that cognition is not the representation of a pre-given world but the activity of a living organism making sense of its environment. Varela drew on biology (the idea of **autopoiesis**, the self-making of living systems) and on Buddhist meditative traditions, an example of the global dialogue you met on Day 87. The **sensorimotor** version of enactivism, defended by Alva Noë (*Action in Perception*, 2004), holds that perception is something we *do*, not something that happens in us. To see a tomato as round is to have implicit mastery of how its appearance would change as you moved around it.

Enactivism challenges the computational picture of Lesson 1 at its core. For Fodor, the mind manipulates internal representations; for radical enactivists such as Daniel Hutto and Erik Myin, basic cognition involves no representations at all, only skilled engagement. A robot built on the enactivist model, like those Rodney Brooks developed at MIT in the 1980s and 1990s, does not build an internal map of the world before acting; it uses the world as "its own best model", reacting to it directly.

sections.heading: How Much Has Changed? Assessing the Debate
sections.body:
Where does all this leave us? It helps to separate three claims, which get progressively stronger.

1. **Dependence.** Human cognition depends heavily on the body and on external tools. Almost no one denies this. Writing, number systems, maps and calendars have transformed what human beings can think.
2. **Embedding.** Cognitive science should study the brain in its environmental and bodily context, because much intelligent behavior arises from brain, body and world working together. This is now mainstream in robotics and much of psychology.
3. **Constitution.** External items can be literal parts of the mind, and the boundary of the self is not fixed by skin and skull. This is the controversial thesis, and the one Clark and Chalmers defended.

Whether the third claim is true matters for more than taxonomy. If Otto's notebook is part of his mind, then stealing it is not merely theft of property but something closer to assault, and reading it without permission is closer to reading his mind. Neil Levy, in *Neuroethics* (2007), drew out such implications under the heading of an **ethical parity principle**: interventions on external parts of the mind deserve the same ethical concern as interventions on the brain.

The debate also connects to personal identity (Lesson 2). If memory is part of what makes you the same person over time, and your memories are partly stored outside your head, then your identity, too, may extend into the world. The worry about outsourcing thought is also ancient. In Plato's *Phaedrus*, Socrates tells a story of the Egyptian god Theuth presenting the invention of writing to King Thamus as a medicine for memory. The king replies that it will do the opposite: those who learn it will stop exercising their memories, relying on external marks, and will have the appearance of wisdom without the reality. It is a striking irony that we know this argument only because Plato wrote it down. Thamus's worry and Clark's optimism are two readings of the same fact: tools change what our minds are. Clark summarized his view in the title of a book: humans are **natural-born cyborgs**, creatures whose minds have always been designed to incorporate tools, from the first written marks to the smartphone.

keyQuote.text: Where does the mind stop and the rest of the world begin?
keyQuote.source: Andy Clark and David Chalmers, 'The Extended Mind', Analysis (1998), opening line

modernConnection.title: Is Your Phone Part of Your Mind?
modernConnection.body:
Chalmers himself drew the obvious modern conclusion. In a foreword to Clark's *Supersizing the Mind* (2008), he reported that he had recently bought an iPhone, which had already taken over some of the central functions of his brain: storing phone numbers, finding his way around, holding his plans. By Clark and Chalmers's own criteria, a smartphone often qualifies. It is reliably available, easily accessed and trusted more or less automatically.

The law has noticed. In *Riley v. California* (2014), the United States Supreme Court ruled unanimously that police generally need a warrant to search a cell phone seized during an arrest. Chief Justice John Roberts observed that phones are now so pervasive in daily life that a visitor from Mars might take them for an important feature of human anatomy, and that searching one can reveal more than searching a house. The court did not adopt the extended mind thesis, but its reasoning moves in that direction: a phone is not like a wallet; it holds the privacies of a life.

Psychology raises a more ambivalent picture. A 2011 study by Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu and Daniel Wegner reported a **Google effect**: when people expect information to be available later online, they remember the information less well but remember better where to find it. On an extended mind view, this is not a failure of memory but a sensible division of labor, just as Otto relies on his notebook. On a more cautious view, we may be outsourcing abilities we should keep, and some research suggests the mere presence of a phone can reduce available attention, though such findings have not always replicated.

AI assistants push the question further. A chatbot that drafts your emails, recalls your past conversations and suggests ideas is more than a notebook: it actively transforms information. Clark has written that such tools might become genuine extensions of our minds, but only if we maintain the right relationship of trust and critical oversight. The real question may not be whether our minds extend, but which extensions make us wiser, and who controls them.

vocabulary.definition: Clark and Chalmers's claim that cognitive processes and mental states can be partly constituted by objects and processes outside the brain and body.
vocabulary.example: According to the extended mind thesis, Otto's notebook is part of his memory.

vocabulary.definition: The principle that if an external process functions in a way that we would count as cognitive if it occurred in the head, it counts as part of the cognitive process.
vocabulary.example: By the parity principle, rotating Tetris pieces on screen counts as part of the player's thinking.

vocabulary.definition: Adams and Aizawa's charge that the extended mind confuses a causal connection to cognition with being part of cognition.
vocabulary.example: Critics allege the coupling-constitution fallacy when someone says a calculator is part of their mind just because they use it.

vocabulary.definition: The view that cognition depends heavily on the environment, while remaining located in the organism.
vocabulary.example: A defender of embedded cognition says your phone helps you remember, but is not part of your memory.

vocabulary.definition: The view that the body and its interactions with the world shape cognition and concepts at a deep level.
vocabulary.example: Embodied cognition explains why we describe ideas as things we can 'grasp' or 'hold'.

vocabulary.definition: The view that cognition is the activity of a living organism making sense of its world through action, rather than the internal representation of a pre-given world.
vocabulary.example: An enactivist says seeing is something you do with your whole body, not a picture formed in the brain.

vocabulary.definition: Meaning that a state has intrinsically, rather than by virtue of being interpreted by someone else.
vocabulary.example: Adams and Aizawa argue that ink in a notebook lacks non-derived content, whereas thoughts have it.

vocabulary.definition: An umbrella term for approaches stressing that cognition is embodied, embedded, enacted and extended.
vocabulary.example: Researchers in 4E cognition study how gestures help children learn math.

thinkingExercise.title: Map Your Extended Mind
thinkingExercise.prompt: Audit the external resources you use to think, remember and decide.
steps: List five external resources you use regularly to remember, calculate, navigate or decide (a phone, notebook, calendar, partner, search engine).
Test each against Clark and Chalmers's four conditions. Which qualify as parts of your mind on their view?
Choose one that qualifies. Imagine losing it suddenly. Describe what you would lose: information, abilities, parts of your identity?
Now argue the other side as Adams and Aizawa or Rupert would. Which description of your relationship with the resource seems more accurate: extension or embedding?
Decide whether there is any resource you would like to rely on less, or more, and explain why in terms of the costs and benefits discussed in this lesson.

summary: Clark and Chalmers's extended mind thesis holds that cognition can extend beyond the head; Otto's notebook plays the same role as Inga's biological memory, and the parity principle says location should not matter.
They proposed conditions for extension: reliable availability, automatic endorsement, easy access and, more tentatively, past conscious endorsement.
Critics charge a coupling-constitution fallacy and demand a mark of the cognitive (Adams and Aizawa), defend an embedded alternative (Rupert), and warn of cognitive bloat.

Embodied cognition and enactivism, rooted in Merleau-Ponty and launched by Varela, Thompson and Rosch, argue that thinking is shaped by bodily action and challenge the computational, representation-based picture of the mind.
The debate has practical consequences for privacy, ethics and identity, as smartphones and AI assistants increasingly function like Otto's notebook.

quiz.question: What is the key similarity between Otto and Inga in Clark and Chalmers's argument?
options: Both rely on a source of stored information that plays the same functional role in guiding action
quiz.explanation: Otto's notebook plays the role for him that biological memory plays for Inga, which is why Clark and Chalmers say both had the belief before consulting their memory.

quiz.question: Which of these best expresses the parity principle?
options: Cognition always happens in the brain
If an external process works like something we would call cognitive inside the head, it is cognitive
All external objects are parts of the mind
quiz.explanation: The parity principle denies that location inside or outside the skull is what makes something cognitive.

quiz.question: On Clark and Chalmers's conditions, a library book you have never read is part of your mind.
quiz.explanation: It fails the conditions of reliable availability, automatic endorsement and past conscious endorsement.

quiz.question: Adams and Aizawa's 'coupling-constitution fallacy' objection says that:
options: Being causally connected to a cognitive process does not make something part of that process
quiz.explanation: They argue that causal coupling with cognition is not enough to make something a constituent of it.

quiz.question: Robert Rupert's alternative to the extended mind is:
quiz.explanation: Rupert holds that cognition depends heavily on the environment but is located within the organism.

quiz.question: Merleau-Ponty's example of a blind man's cane suggests that a well-practiced tool can become part of one's perceptual system.
quiz.explanation: The practiced user perceives through the cane, feeling the ground at its tip, rather than perceiving the cane itself.

quiz.question: Which claim is central to enactivism?
options: The mind is software running on the brain
Cognition is the activity of an organism making sense of its world through action
Meanings are fixed by distant environments
quiz.explanation: Enactivists reject the idea that cognition is the internal representation of a pre-given world.

quiz.question: In Riley v. California, the US Supreme Court explicitly adopted the extended mind thesis.
quiz.explanation: The Court did not adopt the thesis, but its reasoning about the pervasiveness and intimacy of phones moves in a similar direction.

quiz.question: People who expect information to be available online remember it less well but remember where to find it. An extended mind theorist would most likely describe this as:
options: A sensible division of labor between brain and external resources
A refutation of the parity principle
quiz.explanation: On the extended view, this is like Otto relying on his notebook: memory is distributed across brain and world.

goDeeper.body:
One of the most interesting recent developments is the **extended consciousness** debate. Clark and Chalmers were careful to claim that cognitive processes and beliefs can extend, not consciousness. Clark has argued that conscious experience is probably confined to the brain, because it depends on fast, high-bandwidth processes that external loops cannot match. Others disagree. Alva Noë, in *Out of Our Heads* (2009), argued from enactivism that consciousness is not something that happens in us but something we do, and therefore involves body and world essentially. Susan Hurley, in *Consciousness in Action* (1998), had attacked the "classical sandwich" model of the mind, with perception as input, action as output and cognition in the middle, arguing that perception and action are intertwined throughout.

A second debate concerns **socially extended** and **distributed** cognition. The cognitive scientist Edwin Hutchins, in *Cognition in the Wild* (1995), studied navigation on a US Navy ship. He showed that the computation of the ship's position was carried out not by any one person but by a system of people, instruments and charts. No single navigator knew everything; the cognitive system was the team. This raises the question of whether groups, institutions or even societies can have minds of their own, a question with implications for how we think about collective responsibility.

Finally, the **predictive processing** framework, defended by Clark himself in *Surfing Uncertainty* (2016), offers a possible synthesis. On this view, the brain is constantly predicting incoming signals and acting to reduce prediction error, both by updating its models and by changing the world. Clark argues this explains why the brain so readily incorporates external tools: whatever helps reduce prediction error becomes part of the loop. Critics ask whether predictive processing supports extension or, as Jakob Hohwy argues, actually shows the mind to be sealed behind an evidential boundary, the brain's sensory surfaces.

readings.title: The Extended Mind
readings.author: Andy Clark and David Chalmers
readings.note: The original 1998 paper in Analysis; short and readable, with Otto, Inga and Tetris.

readings.title: Natural-Born Cyborgs
readings.author: Andy Clark
readings.note: An accessible book on how humans have always merged with their tools.

readings.title: The Bounds of Cognition
readings.author: Fred Adams and Kenneth Aizawa
readings.note: The most sustained critique of the extended mind.

readings.title: The Embodied Mind
readings.author: Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson and Eleanor Rosch
readings.note: The founding text of enactivism, connecting cognitive science and Buddhist practice.

questions: If someone deleted the notes on your phone without permission, would that be more like stealing your property or damaging your mind?
Can a group of people, such as a ship's crew or a research team, have a mind of its own?
Should we worry that relying on external tools weakens our own abilities, or is that like worrying that writing weakens memory?
